detail.abstract: Our concept of cultural code argues that nations bare certain cultural codes which makes them either more or less competitive on all walks of life. But nations consist of individuals who in their turn might either align with their national cultural codes or disassociate from them under different circumstances and experiences. This paper delves deeper into the definition of culture and offers the 3 dimensional approach towards the studies of cultural codes with a visual model.

title: Beyond Compliance: An Empirical Analysis of the "Red Queen Effect" in NHS Cyber Assurance and the Case for Ecological Rationality
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: Beyond Compliance: An Empirical Analysis of the "Red Queen Effect" in NHS Cyber Assurance and the Case for Ecological Rationality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved the analysis of secondary, publicly available organisational data. No human participants were involved; therefore, ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Objective: To determine if current NHS cybersecurity assurance mechanisms (Data Security and Protection Toolkit — DSPT) accurately reflect governance quality across different organisational scales, and to propose a "velocity-based" alternative (Cyber Progress Measure) that mitigates the "Red Queen Effect". Design: Cross-sectional analysis of NHS Trust financial returns and compliance data for the 2023/24 financial year, combined with a theoretical framework application of evolutionary dynamics and bounded rationality. Setting: NHS Trusts and Foundation Trusts in England (𝑛 = 171). Main Outcome Measures: Correlation between organisational resource capability (Total Staff Costs and WTE) and DSPT compliance status ("Standards Met" vs. "Approaching Standards"). Results: The final cohort comprised 171 Acute, Specialist, and Mental Health Trusts. There was no statistically significant difference in mean staff costs between compliant (£427.0m) and non-compliant (£420.5m) organisations (𝑝 = 0.88; Cohen’s 𝑑 = 0.02). A multivariate logistic regression confirmed that financial resources remained insignificant (𝑝 = 0.92) even when controlling for Foundation Trust status and organisational type. A "complexity ceiling" was evident: while 7.5% of the wider national digital ecosystem achieved "Standards Exceeded," no NHS Trusts in this study cohort attained this level. Paradoxically, the highest- resourced trusts (Q4) demonstrated lower compliance rates (60.5%) than the lowestresourced trusts (Q1, 69.8%), challenging the assumption that scale confers a defensive advantage. Conclusions: Current metrics fail to capture the kinetic effort of defence, penalising large estates that must "run faster" just to stand still. We propose the Cyber Progress Measure (CPM) — a velocity-based heuristic — which aligns with the principle of ecological rationality: in uncertain environments, simple velocity signals outperform complex statebased compliance rules.

title: The Central Bank's Role in Shaping Household Inflation Expectations Through the Media

detail.title: The Central Bank's Role in Shaping Household Inflation Expectations Through the Media

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study relies on the analysis of publicly available text data and aggregate economic indicators; it did not involve human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the influence of central bank communication on media coverage and how this media coverage, in turn, shapes household inflation expectations. I construct text-based indicators that quantify media reporting on inflation and the European Central Bank's (ECB) monetary policy. A novel contribution is the explicit separation between direct quotes from ECB officials and the surrounding journalist commentary, allowing for a distinction between the ECB's own communication and the media's interpretation. Using natural language processing (NLP), I classify more than 2.1 million German newspaper articles as well as ECB press conferences ranging from 2002 to 2023 by sentiment, reported inflation direction, and monetary policy stance. The results suggest that households respond asymmetrically to media signals: they significantly raise their inflation expectations in response to news about rising inflation and dovish ECB quotes cited in the media, but show no statistically significant reaction to news about falling inflation, hawkish ECB quotes, or journalistic commentary regarding monetary policy. Furthermore, I show that the ECB can partially influence this process, as signals of rising inflation in its press conferences have a stronger impact on media reporting than signals of falling inflation.

title: Societal Stigma and Discrimination: The Challenges Faced by Children of Sex Workers Due to Prevailing Attitudes and Lack of Civic Awareness

detail.title: Societal Stigma and Discrimination: The Challenges Faced by Children of Sex Workers Due to Prevailing Attitudes and Lack of Civic Awareness
detail.abstract: The children of sex workers have to navigate social stigma, moral negativity, and systemic neglect that shape their lives in multifarious ways. They bear the social brunt of their mother's occupation. Even when there is no involvement of the children in their mother's profession, children still suffer emotional, social, and educational difficulties. This paper delves into how the stress from the lack of social awareness in the surrounding communities. The impact of the children's mother's profession parallels the children's stigma and the differential treatment that these children suffer in the community. The paper studies the social bias that is most visible in the admission to schools, class rooms, social interaction , and the availability of welfare programs. The consequences of Judgment in the community isolation, identity fragmentation, and social stigma. The paper also illustrates the social and economic pressures that paucity of policies like educational outreach, and civic education that ensnares children in social and economic paradox where there is no escape. The children of sex workers are among the most overlooked and in some cases most marginalised of all social groups in India. Owing to the extreme social stigma around sex work these children are, and continue to be, systemically denied the basic rights to education, healthcare, housing, and social inclusion. This paper looks at the various types and the reasons for, and the impacts of, such forms of discrimination. Particular attention is given to India's largest red-light districts: Sonagachi in Kolkata, Kamathipura in Mumbai, G.B. Road in Delhi, Budhwar Peth in Pune, and the smaller brothel districts of Sangli and Meerut. Based on a review of available literature, including the work of NGOs, legal documentation, and Case Studies in the period of 2005-2025, this paper shows how the indifference of many members of society, including teachers, neighbours, landlords, healthcare workers, and police, contributes to the cycle of oppression and discrimination. This paper makes a number of specific recommendations.

title: Exploring Access to Justice Through the Functioning of Legal Aid Services Authorities in India

detail.title: Exploring Access to Justice Through the Functioning of Legal Aid Services Authorities in India
detail.abstract: Access to justice, recognised as a fundamental human right and guaranteed under Articles 14, 21, and 39A of the Constitution of India, is key to maintaining a democratic and rule-based society. However, India continues to face significant challenges in providing equitable access to its legal system for a population exceeding 1.21 billion. NJDG records show nearly 44.7 million pending cases before District and Taluka courts, indicating that only about four per cent of the population interacts with the justice system at any time. Socio-economic barriers, low legal awareness, high litigation costs, and poor quality of legal representation remain critical obstacles preventing marginalised and vulnerable groups from receiving timely and effective remedies. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, aims to fill these gaps by creating a multi-level network of legal aid institutions at the national, state, district, and taluka levels. Through mechanisms such as Lok Adalats and specialised programs for disaster victims, human trafficking survivors, acid attack victims, undertrial prisoners, senior citizens, and women, the Act encourages accessible and affordable justice. Judicial recognition, notably in Anita Kushwaha v. Pushpa Sudan (2016), further reinforces the constitutional obligation of access to justice. Despite these efforts, numerous challenges, geographical barriers, bureaucratic delays, socio-economic disadvantages, low legal literacy, and inconsistent quality of legal aid continue to impede effective implementation. This research investigates the functioning, impact, and limitations of legal aid authorities in India, assesses their capacity to realise the goal of “Access to Justice for All,” and suggests reforms to strengthen the legal aid system.

title: From Technological Disruption to Institutionalised Assimilation
affiliations: Dhurakij Pundit University

detail.title: From Technological Disruption to Institutionalised Assimilation
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of artificial intelligence (AI) and cyber intelligence (CyINT) becoming increasingly embedded within intelligence systems, the core challenge facing intelligence organisations is no longer ‘whether to adopt new technologies’, but rather ‘how to transform technological disruption into governable, measurable, and trainable institutional capabilities’. This paper examines the proceedings of the Intelligence Studies Summit 2025, published by the National Intelligence University (NIU), to propose the Institutional Absorption Discourse Model (IADM). (Institutional Absorption Discourse Model, IADM). Through computational content analysis, semantic embedding, and longitudinal discourse drift detection, it conducts computable modelling on this academic-practical hybrid corpus—a ‘non-news stream, non-policy text’—comprising conference proceedings. Findings reveal: textual discourse follows a distinct phased progression—‘technological disruption → threat framing → governance and accountability → measurability → education and disciplinary institutionalisation’; governance and accountability discourse significantly lags behind technological topics in sequence yet erupts concentratedly as institutional modules; education and effectiveness measurement constitute stabilisers for institutional absorption. This paper's theoretical contribution lies in translating intelligence discourse into a testable chain of institutional mechanisms. Its methodological contribution proposes a quasi-longitudinal modelling paradigm for conference proceedings, providing an operational pathway for auditing AI governance and intelligence research.

title: E-Waste, Artificial Intelligence, and The Law: Toward A Circular and Sustainable Digital Economy

detail.title: E-Waste, Artificial Intelligence, and The Law: Toward A Circular and Sustainable Digital Economy
detail.abstract: Electronic waste (e-waste) is the fastest-growing global waste stream, projected to exceed 80 million tons annually by 2030. While it contains valuable secondary resources, it also carries hazardous substances that threaten human health, the environment, and the climate. Despite this urgency, regulatory frameworks remain fragmented, with limited progress on right-to-repair initiatives and weak governance of product lifespans. This paper examines the multifaceted impacts of e-waste—including environmental degradation, toxic exposure, economic loss, and illegal trade—and identifies the regulatory gaps driving its escalation. It then explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and Digital Product Passports (DPPs) can strengthen e-waste governance by improving product traceability, enabling predictive maintenance, supporting automated disassembly and sorting, and embedding repairability into consumer choice and policy, illustrated through case studies from the United States and Europe. However, challenges such as incomplete data, infrastructure costs, global inequities, and AI’s own hardware footprint limit effectiveness. The paper concludes that sustainable solutions require combining technological innovation with legal reform and stronger international cooperation—particularly under the Basel Convention—to harmonize standards, close enforcement gaps, and advance a circular and just digital economy.

title: Posted Price and a Knockout Auction: Revenue Maximization Under the Threat of Collusion
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: Posted Price and a Knockout Auction: Revenue Maximization Under the Threat of Collusion
detail.abstract: I explore how a revenue-maximizing principal allocating a single good should optimally design his auction in the presence of collusion. The principal evaluates mechanisms according to the worst-case revenue that could arise from collusive or noncollusive play. The principal's optimal mechanism in the face of collusion is to post a price and run an efficient knockout auction in-house. This remains the optimal mechanism when the principal additionally hypothesizes that colluders are maximizing their joint surplus; with surplus-maximizing colluders, posting a price without running the knockout in-house is also an optimal mechanism.

title: The Impact of Indonesia's Biofuels Policy on the Food and Energy Security
affiliations: Padjadjaran University - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: The Impact of Indonesia's Biofuels Policy on the Food and Energy Security

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: This research critically evaluates the congruence between Indonesia's aggressive biofuels mandatespositioned as a central pillar of national energy security-and its international climate mitigation commitments under the Updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and Net Zero Emission (NZE) frameworks. Employing a recursive dynamic Hybrid Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model integrated with a spatial econometric land-use framework, this study simulates the inter-sectoral economic linkages and deforestation impacts of biofuel expansion scenarios through 2036. The analysis reveals a stark policy dichotomy. While the biodiesel mandate effectively bolsters domestic energy security by increasing the renewable share of the energy supply to approximately 17.44%, it precipitates a detrimental "Food vs. Energy" trade-off that compromises social welfare. Specifically, the expansion drives intense competition for land, inflating land prices for agricultural staples such as rice and other agricultural products by 14-18%, thereby creating inflationary pressure on food systems. Environmentally, the findings demonstrate a critical misalignment between energy policy and climate goals. The study projects that a B-25 blending mandate will induce an average annual deforestation rate of 350,000 hectares by large private plantations alone. This trajectory consumes 77% of Indonesia's total permissible deforestation cap (450,000 hectares/year) under the NDC, rendering the current biofuel strategy fundamentally inconsistent with the Paris Agreement targets. The authors argue that without a decisive shift from extensive land expansion to intensive productivity improvements-targeting yields of 5 tons per hectare-and a rigorous revision of the palm oil moratorium, Indonesia's energy transition will undermine its ecological integrity.

title: Development as Institutional Experiment: Integrating RCTs and SMU's Lessons

detail.title: Development as Institutional Experiment: Integrating RCTs and SMU's Lessons
detail.abstract: This study advances a new paradigm of institutional experimentation in development economics by integrating the experimental precision of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with the institutional dynamics of Korea's Saemaul Undong (SMU). While RCTs offer valuable causal insights, they treat development as a sequence of discrete interventions rather than an evolving system of rules and incentives. The General Theory of Economic Development (GTED) redefines this logic through Economic Differentiation (ED)-a rulebased mechanism that aligns performance, reward, and motivation across state, corporate, and community actors. SMU exemplifies this process: performance-linked incentives, village-level competition, and self-help norms created a self-reinforcing system that eradicated rural poverty within a decade. Building on these lessons, the paper designs a hybrid three-group RCTcontrol, egalitarian, and differentiated-to test institutional rules under identical resource conditions. GTED thus transforms the development paradigm from RCT-based short-term interventions into a process of continuous institutional experimentation and learning.

title: Inflation Targeting and Exchange Rate Predictability in Low-Income Economies

detail.title: Inflation Targeting and Exchange Rate Predictability in Low-Income Economies
detail.abstract: Previous research on the nominal exchange rate (NER) out-of-sample predictability suggests that the current real exchange rate (RER) provides significant evidence in the inflation targeting (IT) adopted advanced economies (AEs) and emerging economies (EMEs). This research fills a gap in the literature by investigating 11 low-income countries (LICs) that adopted IT beginning in the late 2000s. For most LICs, 1-to 48-months ahead out-ofsample exchange rate predictability significantly increases after IT adoption. The results are robust after considering various bootstrapped out-of-sample statistics (e.g. bootstrapped Diebold-Mariano-West (DMW) statistic), forecasting schemes, and impacts from the zero lower bound (ZLB) and COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Price Discrimination with Costless Resale
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Price Discrimination with Costless Resale
detail.abstract: This paper shows that income effects create an endogenous barrier to arbitrage, allowing price discrimination to survive costless resale. A monopolist sells an indivisible good to consumers with heterogeneous incomes who can freely resell. When the good is strictly normal, a consumer's reservation price to resell increases as the purchase price decreases-lower prices leave buyers wealthier and raise their valuation of the good. The monopolist exploits this by subsidising low-income consumers to raise their reservation prices to a target that high-income consumers must also pay. The optimal schedule increases dollar-for-dollar with income in the subsidised segment, weakly dominates uniform pricing, and achieves the first-best allocation when the entire market is served. We show the mechanism extends beyond income effects: low substitutability with market alternatives generates large reservation-price responses even when income sensitivity is modest. Sustaining discrimination requires market power at the individual level-consumer-specific quantity limits-not merely aggregate output restrictions. Extensions examine multiple monopolists and endogenous privacy choices.

title: Iterated elimination in the small and in the large
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Iterated elimination in the small and in the large
detail.abstract: Iterated elimination is often implemented "in the small" as a game reduction procedure: once a strategy is eliminated, it cannot be used as a dominator at later steps. In the actual game, however, eliminated strategies remain feasible. Accordingly, the foundations of most rationalizability and iterated dominance concepts have been established for "in the large" procedures in which eliminated strategies can serve as dominators throughout. This paper provides conditions that guarantee the local-global equivalence in an abstract framework for elimination procedures. Our equivalence connects reduction procedures to epistemic foundations and is technically convenient to establish order independence and other properties of game reductions, which are often easier to prove for "in the large" procedures. We show the broad applicability of our results by analyzing a range of rationalizability and dominance procedures.

title: Shame, Guilt, and Motivated Self-Confidence
affiliations: University of Toulouse 1 - Toulouse School of Economics (TSE),  and Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Shame, Guilt, and Motivated Self-Confidence
detail.abstract: Evidence from anthropology, economics, and psychology indicates that sensitivities to shame and guilt vary substantially across cultures, as does confidence in ability and skills. Is there a connection between these observations? We address this question both theoretically and empirically. Theoretically, we endogenize sensitivities to shame and guilt as well as self-confidence, studying their equilibrium emergence and interactions. Empirically, we find significant evidence of a negative relationship between individual self-confidence and the cultural importance of shame relative to guilt. This relationship holds both across countries and among U.S. immigrants relative to their cultures of origin, exhibiting a long-lasting effect that persists after migration.

title: "Challenges of Statelessness in Indonesia: A Legal Review of Nationality Law, Human Rights, and the Constitutional Obligations of the Indonesian State

detail.title: "Challenges of Statelessness in Indonesia: A Legal Review of Nationality Law, Human Rights, and the Constitutional Obligations of the Indonesian State

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics Approval Statement: This study did not involve patients or human participants, therefore formal ethics approval was not required. The research is based on legal and constitutional analysis conducted independently by the author(s).

detail.abstract: The phenomenon of statelessness represents a pressing legal and humanitarian problem that seriously undermines the fulfillment of fundamental rights for individuals in Indonesia. Although it has received limited public attention, the presence of stateless populations generates intergenerational vulnerabilities, including structural impoverishment, discrimination, family separation, and prolonged detention. This study examines statelessness with a focus on nationality law, human rights, and the constitutional obligations of the state. The discussion covers definitions and various manifestations of statelessness under national regulations and international legal instruments, the underlying causal factors, the social, economic, and human-rights impacts, the vulnerable groups affected, and the legal responses that have been implemented. The analysis centers on the role of the state in ensuring recognition and protection of the constitutional rights of stateless individuals, and it formulates evidence-based policy recommendations to strengthen Indonesia's legal protection and human-rights framework.

title: An Integrated Control-Equilibrium Framework for Socio-Ecological Systems
affiliations: Université Clermont Auvergne, University of Wyoming and University of Lorraine

detail.title: An Integrated Control-Equilibrium Framework for Socio-Ecological Systems

keywords: Conditional Value at Risk JEL codes: C61

detail.abstract: We develop a computable and mathematically rigorous framework for socio-ecological systems (SES) that combines dynamic policy design with decentralized equilibrium behavior. First, we represent the economic, social, and environmental pillars as three coupled networks that interact through stochastic dynamics. Second, we embed decentralized behavior as an instantaneous equilibrium characterized by an evolutionary variational inequality, which delivers a unique and stable response map from policies to private actions. Third, we treat economic, social, and environmental performances as co-equal objectives subject to convex cross-constraints that encode budget feasibility, service and equity floors, environmental quality gates, and tail-risk safeguards based on Conditional Value at Risk. We prove existence of Pareto-efficient policies and equivalence with weighted-sum scalarization under standard convexity and regularity conditions, derive first-order optimality conditions via a stochastic maximum principle with jumps that incorporates equilibrium sensitivities, and obtain a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman characterization in a Markovian subclass. Computation relies on a nested scheme, with fast monotone-operator methods for the equilibrium layer inside a primaldual splitting algorithm that enforces the guarantees. A stylized forestry case study illustrates calibration, the expression of connectivity and reliability targets on a multiplex landscape, and the interpretation of Lagrange multipliers as implementable policy instruments.

title: To converge or not to converge: Accounting for the German reunification
affiliations: University of Kiel and University of Augsburg

detail.title: To converge or not to converge: Accounting for the German reunification
detail.abstract: German reunification in 1990 marked the first sudden integration of a socialist and capitalist economy. Despite East Germany’s (EG) economic catch-up with West Germany (WG), the integration remains unfinished, as indicated by per capita output in EG still being about one-third lower. To study this unfinished regional convergence, we apply wedge-growth accounting using a human capital-augmented, two-sector, two-region model, incorporating labor supply constraints to capture key qualitative differences between EG and WG. Our findings show that sectoral labor and capital wedges are similar within regions and have significantly converged between regions, with EG initially overusing inputs. While productivity in the nontradable goods sector has fully converged, the tradable sector in EG remains less productive than in WG. Counterfactual analysis suggests that this productivity gap, together with persistent net inflows to EG, explains EG’s lower economic activity. However, reducing the inflows would result in significant welfare losses in EG. Furthermore, we account for the reunification event, identifying a substantial productivity catch-up in EG between 1989 and 1991. Our findings offer clear policy insights, highlighting the trade-offs between economic activity and fiscal transfers.

reference: International Journal of Financial Engineering, Vol. 12, No. 04, 2550029 (2025)
title: Modeling credit cycle index for loan loss forecasting under macro-economic scenarios

detail.title: Modeling credit cycle index for loan loss forecasting under macro-economic scenarios

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Financial Engineering, Vol. 12, No. 04, 2550029 (2025)

detail.abstract:
The estimation of future loan losses is not only important for the financial institutions to effectively control the credit risk of commercial loan portfolio, but also an essential component in the capital plan submitted for regulatory approval in the annual stress testing.

This paper describes a methodology of modeling the credit cycle index and estimating the point-in-time (PIT) default and rating migration probabilities based on credit cycle index under macro-economic scenarios. The modeling approach is based on Credit Metrics (1996) and designed to capture the credit risk concentration at the region and industry sector levels for effective stress testing and risk management of credit portfolios. The credit cycle index in the model represents the “hidden” risk factor underlying the default and credit migration with the asset correlation parameter attributed to the default clustering, while the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) of credit cycle index and asset correlation provides a compelling explanation for the original design of risk-weight function used in the calculation of credit risk capital charge under Basel advanced capital model. The credit cycle index generated from the model captures the peak and trough of speculative grade default rates over the long-run historical period, which is consistent with the empirical evidence of credit cycle exhibited for each historical downturn during last 30 years. Furthermore, we apply least-square regression techniques to show the credit cycle index is statistically linked to the macro-economic variables, such as GDP, CPI and Unemployment Rate (UR) which are key economic indicators used by economists to analyze and explain the business cycle. The model establishes a powerful connection between credit cycle and economic cycle which enables the risk manager at large financial institutions to perform stress testing and loss forecasting to effectively control the potential credit loss of loan portfolio under various macro-economic scenarios.

Reliableestimation of extreme credit losses is fundamental for capital adequacy and systemic stability. Traditional Monte Carlo (MC) methods require huge sample sizes as loss probabilities become small1. Extreme‐value models such as the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) and Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution either discard much of the data or depend on subjective thresholds2 【642154988674855 † L352-L356】. Copula‐based extreme value models assume zero tail dependence under Gaussian copulas3, while jump‐diffusion processes are difficult to calibrate4. Adaptive importance sampling (e.g., cross‐entropy) improves efficiency, but the literature notes that high‐ dimensional cases require many samples and suffer from weight degeneracy5.

This paper provides scientific evidence that Sentinel Core, an adaptive rare‐event sampling engine, outperforms these competitors in extreme credit risk estimation. Sentinel Core uses a proprietary algorithm to concentrate sampling in rare loss regions and then applies an unbiased estimator to correct sampling bias. Without divulging proprietary techniques, we show that Sentinel Core delivers higher accuracy, faster convergence and broader failure‐mode coverage than MC, EVT, copula‐EVT, jump‐diffusion and cross‐entropy methods. Our benchmark uses a simulated credit portfolio driven by 20 macro factors with three distinct modes of failure. Under identical computational budgets, Sentinel Core discovers rare events up to 15× faster and produces tail probability estimates roughly 13 %higher thanMC, demonstrating statistically significant improvements.

detail.abstract: Persistent labour-management conflicts often arise from a structural trade-off between organizational efficiency and employee well-being. Existing approaches, such as incentive pay of wellness programs, provide only short-term relief. Adopting a human-centered engineering perspective, this study reconceptualizes capital investment, specifically technological upgrading of production systems, as a systemic intervention to resolve this conflict. Drawing on the marginal product of labor (MPL) framework and self-determination theory, this research analyzes large-scale survey data from 1002 front-line workers and managers in manufacturing firms. The analysis proceeds in two steps: first, correlation and regression analyses are used to establish baseline relationships among key variables; second, a sequential mediation model is established using regression-based mediation analysis. Result demonstrate that technological upgrading reduces working hours and physical intensity, increases work compensation, and consequently strengthens psychological-need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness). These improvements, in turn, significantly decrease turnover intention. Overall, the findings indicate a "triple dividend" of capital investment: improved employee well-being, enhanced organizational performance, and more stable labor-management relations. The study advances theory by linking human-centered systems engineering with psychological need-based models, and offers practical industrial implications by positioning technological upgrading as a systems-level strategy to simultaneously improving productivity and mitigate labor-management conflict.

detail.title: Permit Trading Frictions, Co-Pollutants, and the Case for Cap-and-Trade
detail.abstract: We develop an over-the-counter emissions trading model featuring intermediaries, search and bargaining frictions, firm-specific abatement costs, and localized copollutant damages. Permit prices, volume, and emissions distribution arise endogenously. We examine how market microstructure, abatement cost heterogeneity, and damage functions shape equilibrium outcomes. Contrary to Weitzman (1974), we show that cap-and-trade can outperform a carbon tax because trading frictions compress emissions dispersion across firms, thereby reducing total damages from local copollutants. Calibrated to EU ETS data, optimizing dealer availability reduces deadweight loss to 83% of that under a uniform EU-wide carbon tax, given benchmark discount rate and local damage coefficient.

title: General Equilibrium Amplification and Crisis Vulnerability: Cross-Crisis Evidence from Global Banks
affiliations: University of Tokyo

detail.title: General Equilibrium Amplification and Crisis Vulnerability: Cross-Crisis Evidence from Global Banks
detail.abstract: This paper develops a continuous framework for analyzing financial contagion that incorporates both geographic proximity and interbank network linkages. The framework characterizes stress propagation through a master equation whose solution admits a Feynman-Kac representation as expected cumulative stress along stochastic paths through spatial-network space. From this representation, I derive the General Equilibrium Amplification Factor---a structural measure of systemic importance that captures the ratio of total system-wide effects to direct effects following a localized shock. The amplification factor decomposes naturally into spatial, network, and interaction components, revealing which transmission channels contribute most to each institution's systemic importance. The framework nests discrete cascade models as a limiting case when jump intensity becomes infinite above default thresholds, clarifying that continuous and discrete approaches describe different regimes of the same phenomenon. Empirical validation using 38 global banks across the 2008 financial crisis and COVID-19 pandemic demonstrates that the amplification factor correctly identifies systemically important institutions (Pearson correlation $\rho = -0.450$, $p = 0.080$ between amplification factor and crisis drawdowns) and predicts crisis outcomes out-of-sample ($\rho = -0.352$ for COVID-19). Robustness analysis using cumulative abnormal returns---a measure more directly connected to the Feynman-Kac integral---strengthens these findings ($\rho = -0.512$, $p = 0.042$). Time-series analysis confirms that average pairwise bank correlations track macroeconomic stress indicators ($\rho = 0.265$ with VIX, $p < 0.001$). Comparing the two crises reveals that COVID-19 produced a sharper correlation spike (+93\%) despite smaller equity losses, reflecting different contagion dynamics for exogenous versus endogenous shocks.

title: Pricing Kernel (Non)Monotonicity and Conditional Information
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), Business School, Sun Yat-Sen University, Blockchain Research Center Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Humboldt-University of Berlin and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Pricing Kernel (Non)Monotonicity and Conditional Information
detail.abstract: Estimation of pricing kernels has received substantial attention, particularly following the emergence of the so-called “pricing kernel (PK) puzzle”. Empirical PKs often differ from their theoretical counterparts because the theoretical PK is derived under the risk-neutral measure using a full forward-looking information set, whereas empirical estimates under the physical measure rely only on historical data. A newly proposed Conditional Density Integration (CDI) estimator, designed to reflect forward-looking information sets, aims to produce PKs that align with theory compatible PKs. However, we find that CDI does not fully resolve the issue, because when we compare CDI-estimated PKs with those from traditional methods, both still produce non-monotonic shapes that violate theoretical requirements. One further finding is that the desired monotonicity is highly dependent on the assumption of constant market volatility. The dependency on smoothing parameters further challenges the monotonicity-compliant PK. Empirical tests using S&P 500 and Bitcoin options confirm the impacts of volatility jumps on monotonicity of PK. Our study provides detailed insights into the limitation of PK estimation, which highlights stability of any PK estimations.

title: Enhancing Financial Indicator Predictions with Hybrid Machine Learning:Evidence from Spread, Volatility, and RSI across Global Markets

detail.title: Enhancing Financial Indicator Predictions with Hybrid Machine Learning:Evidence from Spread, Volatility, and RSI across Global Markets
detail.abstract: Technical indicators and volatility measures are fundamental tools for traders and risk managers, yet predicting their future values remains challenging. Traditional machine learning approaches typically attempt to replace established heuristics, often failing to outperform simple baselines. This paper proposes a hybrid framework that incorporates baseline predictions as input features, enabling models to learn when to trust conventional wisdom and when to override it.We evaluate our approach on three financial indicators—bid-ask spread (liquidity), Parkinson volatility (risk), and Relative Strength Index (momentum)—using daily data from 47 global securities across 12 countries from January 2018 to November 2025, spanning four distinct market regimes. Four machine learning models are tested against mean-reversion baselines across 6,345 configurations.Results demonstrate statistically significant improvements for all indicators, with accuracy gains of 2–3 percentage points (p<0.001) and machine learning outperforming baselines in 69–87% of configurations. Consistency across indicators with different underlying dynamics—liquidity, risk, and momentum—suggests that hybrid approaches leveraging domain knowledge as features offer a generalizable framework for financial prediction.

title: The 2024 NAR Ruling and Housing Market Dynamics: Short-Term Evidence from St. Paul
affiliations: Macalester College - Department of Economics and University of Minnesota Twin Cities

detail.title: The 2024 NAR Ruling and Housing Market Dynamics: Short-Term Evidence from St. Paul
detail.abstract: On August 17, 2024, a court ruling restructured real estate market practices by prohibiting the concealment of agent commission rates on multiple listing services and requiring buyer contracts to disclose commission fees. Because commissions function as intermediary transaction costs, the ruling was anticipated to reduce these costs and enhance market efficiency. Using transaction level data on single-family home sales in St. Paul, Minnesota, between May and November 2024, we implement a difference-in-differences framework to estimate the short-term effects of the ruling on housing market outcomes, including prices, liquidity, transaction frictions, and the efficiency of price discovery. The results show no statistically significant short-term effects of the ruling on either home prices or market efficiency. Robustness checks using non-single-family properties, alternative treatment and control groups based on price segments, and neighborhood-level analyses of single-family homes corroborate these findings.

title: Is Bitcoin a Lucky Survivor?

detail.title: Is Bitcoin a Lucky Survivor?
detail.abstract: This paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate subjective crash probabilities for 31 traditional and alternative asset classes using monthly data from 2000-2024. Building on the rare-disaster asset-pricing structure of Binsbergen, Hua, Peeters, and Wachter (2025), we adapt the framework to a higher-frequency, cross-asset setting, which provides additional information about downside realizations without altering the core economic mechanism. Embedding the inferred crash beliefs into the model yields a decomposition of realized returns into learning, driven by revisions in perceived crash risk, and luck, driven by cash-flow shocks. The model generates expected returns that track medium-horizon dynamics and attain empirically plausible magnitudes. For U.S. equities, the wedge between realized and expected returns approaches the historical equity premium and is largely explained by persistent declines in crash beliefs. Bitcoin exhibits expected returns that exceed realized outcomes, whereas U.S. technology equities display a positive wedge primarily attributable to luck. Across asset classes, the framework produces intuitive patterns aligned with differences in tail exposure and helps account for heterogeneous performance episodes.

detail.title: Surviving the Shock: Financial Risk and Minority Ventures During COVID-19
detail.abstract: Using longitudinal data from the National Establishment Time-Series (NETS) and a Cox proportional hazards model, this study examines how financial risk shaped the survival of minority-owned ventures during the COVID-19 pandemic. We find that higher pre-crisis financial risk significantly increased the likelihood of firm exit, indicating that constrained access to credit limited business resilience during the crisis. Minority-owned ventures were disproportionately vulnerable, reflecting persistent structural barriers in credit markets. Firms engaged in international trade and those located in metropolitan areas faced elevated exit risks due to supply-chain disruptions and higher operating costs. In contrast, newer ventures exhibited greater resilience, consistent with greater organizational flexibility and faster adoption of digital tools and remote work. These findings highlight how financial vulnerability and adaptive capacity jointly determined business survival, with implications for inclusive financing and crisis-responsive support.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines a structural vulnerability in the financial architecture of the contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) sector: the capitalization of contingent equity and interdependent growth assumptions as if they were independent and durable sources of firm value. AI-related firms increasingly hold equity-linked instruments—such as warrants, investment rights, or strategic stakes—whose economic value depends on ecosystem-wide growth and future performance, not on present cash flows.

While these instruments comply with accounting standards, their capitalization introduces correlation risk and procyclical exposure. When growth expectations weaken at any critical node—whether a supplier, investor, or infrastructure partner—probability-weighted valuations can cascade across multiple firms’ balance sheets simultaneously, even without fraud or insolvency. This mechanism may accelerate synchronized repricing and systemic devaluation.

Drawing historical parallels to the 2000 dot-com collapse and the structural dynamics of the 2008 financial crisis, the paper argues that AI-sector valuations may be more fragile than commonly assumed. Even a modest downgrade in forward assumptions could plausibly result in trillion-dollar equity losses, not through cash destruction but through expectation withdrawal.

title: Battle of the markups: conflict inflation and the aspirational channel of monetary policy transmission
affiliations: Bank of England and University of Oxford

detail.title: Battle of the markups: conflict inflation and the aspirational channel of monetary policy transmission
detail.abstract: Since the post-Covid rise in inflation has been accompanied by strong wage growth, the distributional conflict between wage- and price-setters (both wishing to attain a certain markup) has regained prominence. We examine how a central bank should resolve a “battle of the markups” when desired markups are cyclically sensitive, highlighting how monetary policy can transmit by affecting markup aspirations. We establish conditions under which above-target inflation requires a reduction in economic activity, to eliminate worker-firm disagreement over the appropriate level of the real wage. We show that countercyclical markups and/or a flat Phillips curve call for more dovish monetary policy. Following an adverse cost-push shock, optimal policy might even call for a period of joint price and wage inflation.

title: Machine Learning Integrated Tail Risk Detection: Combining GARCH Volatility Dynamics, Extreme Value Theory, and Gradient Boosting for Crisis Prediction

detail.title: Machine Learning Integrated Tail Risk Detection: Combining GARCH Volatility Dynamics, Extreme Value Theory, and Gradient Boosting for Crisis Prediction
detail.abstract: Traditional Value at Risk models systematically failed during the 2008 financial crisis, underestimating tail risk through static volatility assumptions and backward-looking calibration. This paper introduces a machine learning integrated framework that transforms econometric models, specifically GARCH volatility dynamics and Extreme Value Theory parameters, into engineered features for supervised tail risk prediction. Rather than estimating current VaR values, we reframe the problem as predicting whether future returns will exceed VaR thresholds, enabling integration of multiple risk signals into a unified early warning system. Using daily returns from five major U.S. investment banks during 2005-2010, we train an XGBoost classifier to predict tail events, achieving 60.1% AUC on in-sample data with performance improving to 64.2% during the crisis period. Out-ofsample validation on the COVID-19 market crash achieves 73.5% AUC, representing a 22.3% improvement over in-sample performance despite no exposure to pandemic-era data during training. SHAP analysis reveals that GARCH conditional volatility dominates predictions with 21.8% importance, while novel interaction features capturing volatility and cross-sectional dispersion rank second at 14.1%, detecting systemic stress propagation that isolated models miss. Statistical validation includes Chow tests confirming structural breaks, Kupiec and Christoffersen backtests demonstrating traditional VaR failures, and robustness analysis across threshold specifications. The framework contributes to quantitative risk management by providing an interpretable, regime-adaptive screening tool for risk committees.

detail.abstract: In single image 3D reconstruction, the occlusion often hinders the completereconstruction of objects. A point cloud reconstruction method is presented thatleverages fine-grained features from a single RGB image, named OFGNet. By adopting a block-based approach to enhance thefusion weight of visible parts in occluded images, the accuracy of image retrieval isimproved. Additionally, OFGNet designs a point cloud reconstruction network basedon skip connections and residual connections for 3D point cloud reconstruction from asingle image. By employing skip connections and residual connections, the networkenhances the features of the retrieved point cloud, achieving highly accurate pointcloud reconstruction results. This method is also evaluated on both synthetic andreal-world datasets, and experimental results validate its effectiveness.

detail.abstract: The effects of student on educational outcomes are well documented, with most studies showing a significant, negative effect on student performance. In recent years, a growing number of institutions have been using a variety of nudge interventions to help combat absenteeism, improve student performance, and reduce dropout rates. Although many studies report the success of many of these initiatives in terms of student performance and retention, others alert that nudging can also have significant negative effects on students. This paper examines the effectiveness of nudging undergraduate students to improve attendance and student performance in tutorial sessions. We conducted a quasi-natural experiment with more than 400 year two UK university students, randomly assigning them to either a treatment group receiving personalized email reminders after missing tutorials, or a control group without any nudging intervention. Our results show a large and significant positive effect of the nudging intervention on attendance rates. Furthermore, using a two-stage least squares estimation method, we established that improved tutorial attendance leads to better performance. Our findings advance the debate on the efficacy of nudges in higher education and offer some important insights for addressing student absenteeism at the university level.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relevance of banks’ exposure to climate transition risk in the interbank lending market. Using transaction-level data on repo agreements, we first establish that banks with higher exposure to transition risk face significantly higher borrowing costs. This premium is a combination of a risk premium, compensating lenders for increased credit risk, and an inconvenience premium, reflecting the sustainability preferences of key dealer banks. We also find that the transition risk premium intensifies during periods of financial stress, indicating that climate-induced risks amplify existing vulnerabilities in financial markets. Furthermore, the rate segmentation caused by transition risk premium has implications for the transmission of monetary policy. Transition risk is an important factor in financial stability and policy design.

detail.abstract: We use a novel data set containing all corporate loans throughout the Eurozone to document a series of novel stylized facts on the relationship between collateral and the probability of default. First, we show that the pervasive empirical finding that riskier borrowers pledge collateral is driven by economists’ informational disadvantage relative to banks. Accounting for time-varying bank- and firm-specific risk factors produces negative correlations consistent with theory. Second, the relationship between pledging collateral and the probability of default is non-linear. Increasing the ex-ante collateral-to-loan ratio initially lowers the default likelihood but increases it as loans become overcollateralized. Third, this is driven by the riskiness of collateral. We estimate that an increase in the ex-ante collateral-to-loan ratio correlates with greater variance in the underlying collateral’s market value after loan origination. We develop a model featuring risk-neutral agents and risky collateral that provides intuition for these empirical patterns. Pledging risky collateral lowers lenders’ expected returns in case of default, leading them to demand more collateral to originate a loan but this diminishes a borrower’s return when a project is successful leading to less effort and a higher probability of default.

detail.abstract:
Several countries have implemented a carbon tax or cap-and-trade system to establish high carbon prices and create a disincentive for the use of fossil fuels. Essentially, the tax encourages firms to substitute toward low carbon emission energy. Costs also rise for firms down the supply chain that use production inputs with high-emission content, so the total impact of a carbon tax can be large. In practice, however, firms also have an incentive to find an offset to a carbon tax. In this post, based on our recent work, we present evidence of one such adaptation strategy. We show that French firms increased their imports of high-emission inputs from suppliers outside the European Union’s cap-and-trade system, known as the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), reducing the effectiveness of this approach to cutting carbon emissions—an adaptation strategy that leads to “carbon leakage.” To help stop this leakage, the EU is implementing a “carbon tariff” in 2026, which is the topic of a companion post.

detail.abstract:
The European Union has been an early adopter of carbon policies, with the introduction of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) in 2005. This scheme sets a common price for carbon and is applied to the most polluting manufacturing sectors. By increasing the cost of emissions-intensive production, the system incentivizes firms to decrease their use of fossil fuels. However, as we show in a companion post, the policy’s impact was moderated by firms increasing their reliance on high-emissions imports. To eliminate this workaround, the EU will expand the ETS to imports in 2026, through the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The CBAM will essentially put a tariff on imported goods based on their carbon content. Our recent work provides a quantitative analysis of how the ETS and CBAM affect firms’ supply choice decisions, and the resulting changes in domestic prices and emissions.

title: Beyond the Balance Sheet: A Discussion of Koenig et al.'s (2026) "Generating Societal Value from Natural Capital on Corporate-Owned Land"

detail.title: Beyond the Balance Sheet: A Discussion of Koenig et al.'s (2026) "Generating Societal Value from Natural Capital on Corporate-Owned Land"
detail.abstract: The growing adoption of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA) reflects efforts to integrate environmental considerations into corporate decision-making by rendering ecosystem services economically visible, particularly in land-constrained and biodiverse contexts such as Small Island Developing States (SIDS). Koenig et al. (2026) make a timely contribution by applying Corporate Natural Capital Accounting (CNCA) to compare alternative land-use scenarios on a large corporate-owned estate in Mauritius, showing that a low-density "Agrihood" development can generate substantial societal value while remaining financially profitable. While acknowledging the analytical rigor and applied relevance of their CNCA framework, this Discussion examines the policy, governance, and valuation implications of defining "societal value" primarily through monetary and utilitarian metrics. It argues that monetized valuation risks marginalizing non-market dimensions-such as cultural heritage, social equity, and relational human-nature values-that are central to societal well-being yet poorly captured by accounting-based approaches. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature in environmental economics, policy analysis, and social science, the Discussion advocates a pluralistic natural capital framework that complements CNCA with qualitative and spatially explicit community value mapping, embedded within supportive policy and institutional arrangements. The analysis further highlights the limits of voluntary, corporate-led NCA adoption in the absence of governance mechanisms that align private decision-making with socially optimal land-use outcomes.

detail.abstract: Europe is already feeling the effects of a rapidly warming climate. Higher temperatures and severe floods, windstorms and wildfires have become defining features of recent years. But what this means for macroeconomic stability and policy is not fully understood. To shed more light on how extreme weather events affect the economy, we combine macroeconomic data at the most detailed regional level and at the highest temporal frequency available with high-resolution meteorological information for Spain’s continental provinces (NUTS-3 regions) from 2000 to 2022. This approach addresses the identification constraints and aggregation biases that have limited previous evidence. Panel local projections show that floods and windstorms trigger substantial and persistent contractions in real regional output per capita, while effects of wildfires are more limited. Extending our analysis to state-dependent local projections, we find that regions with high capital density, limited fiscal space or low insurance coverage see deeper and more persistent output declines, especially after floods. Thus, the effects of extreme weather events are genuine macroeconomic shocks in terms of their size and persistence. Sustained reconstruction support, broader insurance coverage, and targeted adaptation measures are hence crucial to increase macroeconomic resilience in the face of rising climate risks.

detail.abstract: Healthcare compliance programs have traditionally focused on documentation integrity, billing accuracy, and credentialing oversight. While these mechanisms remain essential, they are insufficient to detect a growing category of risk embedded in everyday clinical operations: informal nursing conduct occurring outside formal documentation processes. Modern nursing practice is increasingly shaped by high patient-contact frequency, informal oral communication, social media visibility, and reduced supervisory presence. As a result, boundary erosion, casual patient objectification, and informal disclosures may become normalized without triggering traditional compliance alerts. This paper argues that healthcare organizations must expand compliance infrastructure beyond chartbased audits to include observation-based behavioral oversight focused on nursing practice. Drawing on professional ethics standards, patient-safety literature, and contemporary operational realities, the paper proposes structured, non-punitive observation mechanisms designed to identify cultural drift before harm occurs. Positioned as a companion to existing frameworks for documentation governance and body-worn camera policy, this analysis demonstrates why informal nursing conduct represents a critical and underregulated dimension of modern healthcare risk.

detail.abstract: Suicide is often an impulsive act, and in the United States, nearly one-half of suicides involve a firearm, the most lethal and readily available method. In this paper, we use recent developments in difference-indifferences methodology to study the causal effect of waiting-period laws on firearm suicides. We find that waiting periods reduce firearm suicides among men by 1.5 deaths per 100,000 population, an 11% decrease from baseline. For white individuals, we observe a statistically significant reduction of 37.5 deaths per 100,000, a 37% decrease. For adults aged 55 and older, we find a reduction of 25 deaths per 100,000, representing a 40% decrease. For the overall population, we find a statistically significant reduction of 0.92 deaths per 100,000, a 12% decrease from baseline. Crucially, we find no evidence of substitution toward non-firearm suicide methods following waiting period adoption; among men, adults 55 and older, and white individuals, we find significant decreases in non-firearm suicides. We also examine the effects of waiting period repeal and find statistically significant increases in firearm suicides. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest waiting periods prevented approximately 3,000 firearm suicide deaths annually, yielding social benefits of roughly $41 billion. Our findings show that even brief delays in firearm access can disrupt the pathway from suicidal ideation to death, suggesting that cooling-off periods may be an important policy tool for suicide prevention.

——A Construction of Ideological System Based on the Essence of Political Economy
detail.abstract: Starting from the simple perception of people's livelihood prices, this paper penetrates the superficial financial accounting and economic model myths and directly addresses the core contradiction of the concentrated outbreak of implicit costs in China’s economic development model, constructing an ideological system of monetary sovereignty and debt restructuring in extraordinary times with People-Oriented Nature as the core. Breaking away from the path dependence of traditional fiscal and taxation reform, this paper redefines sovereign currency as a People’s Contract, debunks the Accounting Illusion of "bank credit exhaustion", and demonstrates that debt restructuring under the modern sovereign credit system is essentially a political decision rather than a mere financial issue. It diagnoses that overdraft growth with real estate as the credit amplifier is essentially the rupture of an Implicit Social Contract, where residents overdraw decades of future consumption to finance public investment, and the mortgage crisis is the unfair sharing of development costs in essence. This paper proposes a Political Surgery scheme led by national sovereign credit, realizing the mandatory renegotiation of the broken Implicit Social Contract through targeted Debt Socialization—shifting the unfair costs from residents’ private balance sheets back to the national public balance sheet. Ultimately, it focuses on the ethical choice of choosing the lesser of two evils in governance, taking the value orientation of monetary sovereignty application as the ultimate touchstone for testing the People-Oriented Nature of the regime. Breaking away from the shackles of Western monetary and debt theories, this paper provides a Chinese indigenous solution to systemic debt crises, an ethical compass for the fair sharing of development costs, and anchors the essential logic that national credit serves people’s well-being. It fills the research gap of China’s indigenous monetary sovereignty theoretical system, enriches the core connotation of socialist political economy with Chinese characteristics, and possesses important theoretical originality and practical value for national governance.

detail.abstract: Despite growing adoption and regulatory progress, significant concerns and doubts persist regarding the reliability and future of cryptocurrencies. In recent years, the cryptocurrency landscape has evolved substantially, marked by key developments such as the approval of Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH) exchange-traded funds (ETFs). These milestones may indicate a shift in the trajectory of cryptocurrencies, potentially altering their value, characteristics, and role in financial systems. This study investigates the validity of earlier empirical research through a replication analysis of four key studies. With this approach, one may assess whether earlier findings on asset class classification, portfolio allocation, fundamental valuation, and speculative bubbles of cryptocurrency market remain valid over a longer time period. Evaluating the robustness and relevance of previous studies is crucial, as it can help make more informed decisions within the rapidly evolving environment of digital assets. The results show that the earlier findings are still valid and demonstrate stability over time. As regimes and cycles evolve, our replications show that although "Crypto Currency Returns" fluctuate significantly, the story ultimately resolves toward Crypto Currency "Returns".

detail.abstract: The livestock sector faces global environmental, health, and socioeconomic challenges, requiring a shift towards more equitable and sustainable futures. Understanding academic literature on sustainable livestock futures is key to navigating the contested discourse across policy, practice, and society. This study takes a novel approach, combining topic modelling with framing analysis to explore the topic framing, thematic trends, and regional distribution of sustainable livestock futures research. This combined method offers a replicable, efficient way to navigate complex discourse and contested debates. We find literature remains dominated by techno-scientific and economic framings that prioritise emissions reduction, environmental management, productivity, and efficiency. These framings offer a narrow interpretation of sustainability, often overlooking deeper systemic issues related to equity, justice, and the role of consumption-side interventions, despite some growing interest in dietary shifts in recent years. The study also highlights the notable influence of the US, UK, and China in global livestock systems research, with major funding bodies and influential journals prioritising dominant narratives. Alternative framings and regionally tailored approaches remain underexplored and underfunded, highlighting imbalance in research priorities. Dominant narratives risk reinforcing incumbent systems, highlighting the need for more transformative, inclusive, and systemic research approaches.

detail.abstract: Markowitz Portfolio Theory (MPT) provides a normative framework for portfolio choice but falls short of capturing the heterogeneity of real-world investor behaviours. Recent research shows that two principles-Subjective Allocation Rule (SAR) and Minimum Tracking Error (MTE)-suffice to reconcile such heterogeneity within a single framework. This paper advances the argument from parsimony to completeness by establishing an axiomatic foundation that identifies allocation and mimicking as the two mutually exclusive atoms of active portfolio selection, and shows how SAR and MTE jointly explain, unify, and guide practices. The result is a practical, behaviour-consistent generalisation of MPT: a Unified Portfolio Theory.

detail.abstract: This paper compares models trained with classification algorithm with those trained using regression algorithm. We use technical indicators, 43 bond characteristics and 94 stock characteristics as predictors. We find very strong evidences of the superior predictive ability of classification models over regression models for bonds. All machine learning models for classification algorithm have statistically significant mean returns, unlike regression algorithm, in which only 3 out of 10 models are statistically significant. Classification models have significantly better results for the evaluation metric; mean bond return, alpha intercept, cumulative return, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, zero return BETC and insignificant BETC. For stocks, we do not find strong evidences of the predictive advantage of classification models over regression model. For bonds, classification models are able to exploit the information contained in bond characteristics besides technical indicators, unlike regression models, therefore leading to significantly better results.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly use goal transparency as a management tool, yet little is known about how social comparison of self-set goals-rather than performance outcomes-affects ambition and productivity. We address this gap by investigating whether providing goal rank feedback leads to more ambitious targets that enhance productivity or distort goal-setting in ways that ultimately undermine performance. Using a real-effort laboratory experiment, we randomly assign participants to treatments varying in the availability and public visibility of goal rank information (no ranking, private ranking, or public ranking). We find that goal-rank feedback significantly increases goal levels but reduces performance. The negative effect of goal-rank feedback operates almost exclusively through women's responses. Despite similar upward goal adjustments by both genders, both private and public rank feedback reduce the performance and earnings of women but increase that of men. These gender differences in outcomes arise from divergent effort reallocation patterns: While both women and men maintain similar accuracy rates, men modestly increase their number of attempts in response to ranking information, whereas women significantly reduce theirs. Our findings reveal that transparency in goal-setting can create a wedge between ambition and execution, with particularly adverse consequences for women. Organizations should therefore consider the potential for goal transparency to backfire, especially in gender-diverse settings where unintended disparities may emerge.

title:
The Secret of President Park Chung Hee's Korean Miracle: 

An Emergent Development Perspective

detail.title:
The Secret of President Park Chung Hee's Korean Miracle: 

An Emergent Development Perspective
detail.abstract:
This paper unveils the secret behind South Korea’s economic miracle under President Park Chung Hee,
who transformed an impoverished agrarian society into a major industrial economy in under 20 years
through economic differentiation (ED). By aligning markets, corporations, and government to prioritize
performance-based incentives, Park’s policies—export promotion, heavy chemical industrialization
(HCI), and the Saemaul Undong—fostered a self-reliant, competitive spirit, driving nonlinear order-
transforming, emergent development rooted in complexity economics. His corporate-led prosperity
paradigm nurtured small and medium enterprises (SMEs) into global conglomerates, defying
mainstream neoclassical and socialist economic theories that criticize his approach as authoritarian or
market-distorting. Despite sacrificing short-term democracy via the Yushin regime to achieve long-term
prosperity, Park’s foresight in leveraging ED and anticipating complexity science principles, such as
synergy and the butterfly effect, offers a transformative model for nations seeking economic catch-up
or recovery from stagnation. This study critiques the misattribution of Korea’s success to export-led
growth based on comparative advantage, highlighting Park’s strategic industrial policies and contrasting
his achievements with modern global challenges of low growth and polarization in democratic market
economies, proposing his ED-based approach as a blueprint for global economic revitalization.

title: Institutions, Growth, and Distribution

detail.title: Institutions, Growth, and Distribution
detail.abstract: This paper examines institutional requirements for economic development within democracymarket systems using the General Theory of Economic Development (GTED). GTED posits that growth and inequality stem from institutional functionality-economic differentiation (ED) versus economic egalitarianism (EE)-rather than regime type. ED rewards verifiable performance via markets, corporations, and governments, boosting incentives, innovation, and productivity. EE distributes resources uniformly, weakening motivation and leading to stagnation. A dynamic model formalizes ED's technology amplification (θ > 1) and EE's erosion (θ < 1), yielding shared growth or polarized stagnation. Empirical analysis of panel data from 66 countries (2005-2013) across non-democracy-market (NDM), young (YDM), advancing (ADM), and mature democracy-market (MDM) stages confirms GTED: ED drives GDP growth and reduces inequality in non-mature regimes, while EE induces low growth and rising polarization in MDM. Controls for corporate concentration, openness, and schooling reinforce findings. GTED critiques regime-focused theories, extending Schumpeter and New Institutional Economics by emphasizing corporations' role in ED. Policy implications advocate performance-based reforms in industrial, financial, and welfare systems to sustain prosperity in democracies.

detail.abstract: The idea that labor scarcity can induce economic development has long been hypothesized, but the evidence remains limited. This paper examines how the Second Great Migration (1940-1970) spurred structural change in the American South between 1970 and 2010. Empirical results using shift-share instruments show that out-migration incentivized capital investment and capital-augmenting technical change in the South that lost workers, increasing capital per worker and output in both agriculture and manufacturing. Labor was further reallocated from agriculture to manufacturing and local services. I then develop a dynamic spatial general equilibrium model that incorporates substitution between factors of production, factor-biased technical change, and factor abundance-based trade to characterize this process. The quantitative analysis indicates that labor-capital substitution played a major role in the adjustments to South-to-North migration.

detail.abstract:
Problem & Motivation: For decades, mainstream macroeconomics has struggled to explain persistent development puzzles: why financially deep economies stagnate while banking-scarce ones surge, why financial literacy programs yield inconsistent results, and why similar policies produce asymmetric outcomes across nations. This research identifies the root cause: a fundamental blind spot in economic theory—the demography of organizations. We propose that economies are not mere aggregates of capital and labor, but complex organizational ecosystems whose gender composition and reproductive vitality dictate their growth, stability, and development trajectories.
Theoretical Innovation: This paper introduces a transformative theoretical and empirical framework that re-envisions macroeconomics through the lens of Organizational Taxonomy. We classify all economic entities into four gendered-demographic categories: Male (financial intermediaries), Female (productive enterprises), Barren (non-profit/government), and Non-Barren (for-profit entities). From this taxonomy, we derive the κ-ratio—the female-to-male organizational ratio—as a primal macroeconomic state variable. We demonstrate mathematically and empirically that deviation of κ from an optimal range (1,400–1,800) determines national economic destinies.
Methodological Breakthrough: We deploy the first integrated mixed-methods architecture in macroeconomic research: (1) Agent-Based Modeling explores complex organizational dynamics and identifies critical thresholds; (2) Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium formalizes equilibrium and welfare implications; (3) Econometric analysis tests predictions on a novel 120-country panel dataset (1990–2023); and (4) Comparative case studies provide deep contextual validation for Tanzania (extreme imbalance) and Germany (advanced equilibrium).
Empirical Findings: The global economy is in profound 327% organizational disequilibrium. The world κ-ratio stands at 6,830 versus an optimal 1,600. Correcting this requires the largest financial sector expansion in history: 2.97 million new banks and $29.7 trillion investment over 20 years. Our analysis reveals that:
•
The NB/B ratio (Non-Barren/Barren) is the strongest predictor of GDP growth (β = +0.247, p=0.023)
•
The κ-ratio exhibits an inverted-U relationship with stability
•
Financial literacy gaps enhance stability only when κ is low; in financially dense economies, they become destabilizing
•
Tanzania suffers 14,900% disequilibrium (κ = 225,000 vs optimal 1,500)
Policy Transformation: Achieving optimal organizational balance would unlock: 50% increase in global GDP (from $105 to $157.5 trillion), 180 million new jobs, and lift 500 million people from poverty. For Tanzania specifically, establishing 8,400 banks (from 56) would catalyze sustainable 9.2% GDP growth, elevate financial stability from 0.41 to 0.92, and generate welfare gains equivalent to a 164% permanent consumption increase.
Paradigm Shift: We propose nothing less than a complete inversion of economic governance: from price/output targeting to organizational balance targeting. Our policy invention includes κ-targeting monetary policy, gender-aware macroprudential rules, and spatial banking standards (e.g., 1 bank per 7,738 people in Tanzania) as mandatory instruments. This represents the birth of "Organizational Macroeconomics"—a new field where economic health is measured not by inflation or unemployment alone, but by the balance, literacy, and reproductive vitality of an economy's organizational ecosystem.
Contribution & Implications: This research provides the first unified framework integrating organizational ecology, demographic principles, and financial literacy into macroeconomic theory. It bridges micro-organizational behavior with macro-financial outcomes, offers empirically-validated development roadmaps, and establishes the κ-ratio as a fundamental economic variable with greater explanatory power than traditional indicators. The implications redefine economic planning, financial inclusion, and development strategy for the 21st century, offering a mathematically rigorous pathway to a more stable, prosperous, and balanced world economy.

detail.abstract: Can governments counter populist movements through public goods provision? We examine this question using Biden's Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the 2022 US congressional elections. Combining district-level infrastructure spending data with election results and individuallevel survey data from the 2022 Cooperative Election Study, we test whether targeted public investment can reduce support for populist candidates. We find that infrastructure spending reduced Republican vote share, but this effect was dramatically amplified in districts where (1) infrastructure needs were highly visible (poor bridges) and (2) Trump endorsed the Republican candidate. In high-need districts, infrastructure spending reduced vote share for Trump-endorsed candidates by approximately 5 percentage points more than non-endorsed candidates. This pattern reveals a fundamental tension in populist politics: populist leaders oppose government spending ideologically, even when their constituents desperately need public goods. Our findings suggest that well-targeted public goods provision can effectively counter populist movements by exposing the gap between populist rhetoric and material delivery, contributing to debates about how democracies can respond to the populist challenge.

detail.abstract: Does democracy improve the quality of ministerial selection? A common view is that electoral competition produces more competent leaders and broadens the social backgrounds of political elites. Using newly compiled data on ministerial backgrounds in 141 countries from 1966 to 2015 with an event-study difference-indifference estimator, I examine how transitions to democracy alter the composition of executive cabinets. I find little evidence that democracies appoint more highly educated ministers, though they do replace individuals with military/police backgrounds with prior political experience. Democracy modestly reduces the share of ministers from upper-class occupational backgrounds, but this shift does not broaden professional diversity. Over the longer run, democracy is associated with a slight increase in ministers with political family ties, but not with greater regional favoritism. Overall, the effects of democracy on elite selection are more modest than often assumed, and patterns of elite persistence remain strong.
